final_proof:
As stated, the claim is false under the sole hypothesis that \(f\) is integrable. For example, take \(f(x)=|x|\) on \([-1,1]\) and \(n=1\). The trapezium approximation is \(T_1=\frac{2}{2}(f(-1)+f(1))=2\), whereas \(\int_{-1}^{1}|x|\,dx=1\). At every point where \(f''\) exists it equals \(0\), and at \(0\) it does not exist, so there is no \(\xi\in[-1,1]\) for which the asserted positive expression equals the nonzero signed error \(T_1-\int_{-1}^{1}f=1\). (Indeed, for a general integrable function the displayed expression need not even be defined.)

The standard corrected statement is the following. Suppose \(a<b\), \(n\geq 1\), and \(f\in C^2([a,b])\). Put \(h=(b-a)/n\), \(x_r=a+rh\), and
\[
T_n=\frac h2\left(f(x_0)+f(x_n)+2\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}f(x_r)\right).
\]
Then there is \(\xi\in[a,b]\) such that
\[
T_n-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=\frac{(b-a)^3}{12n^2}f''(\xi).
\]
Thus the formula in the question is correct when "error" means approximation minus exact value; if error is defined as exact value minus approximation, its negative must be used.

To prove the corrected statement, fix a subinterval \([u,v]=[x_{r-1},x_r]\), so that \(v-u=h\), and define
\[
K_r(x)=\frac12(x-u)(v-x)\qquad (u\leq x\leq v).
\]
We have \(K_r(u)=K_r(v)=0\), \(K_r'(u)=h/2\), \(K_r'(v)=-h/2\), and \(K_r''=-1\). Two integrations by parts therefore give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_u^v K_r(x)f''(x)\,dx
&=-\int_u^v K_r'(x)f'(x)\,dx\\
&=-[K_r'(x)f(x)]_u^v+\int_u^v K_r''(x)f(x)\,dx\\
&=\frac h2\bigl(f(u)+f(v)\bigr)-\int_u^v f(x)\,dx.
\end{aligned}
\]
Summing this identity for \(r=1,\ldots,n\), the endpoint terms combine to give exactly the composite trapezium sum, and hence
\[
T_n-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=\int_a^b K(x)f''(x)\,dx,
\]
where \(K\) agrees with \(K_r\) on each subinterval. The function \(K\) is continuous and nonnegative on \([a,b]\). Since \(f''\) is continuous, the weighted mean-value theorem for integrals yields some \(\xi\in[a,b]\) such that
\[
\int_a^b K(x)f''(x)\,dx=f''(\xi)\int_a^b K(x)\,dx.
\]
Finally, on every subinterval,
\[
\int_u^v K_r(x)\,dx=\frac12\int_0^h t(h-t)\,dt=\frac{h^3}{12}.
\]
Consequently
\[
\int_a^b K(x)\,dx=\frac{nh^3}{12}=\frac{(b-a)^3}{12n^2}.
\]
Substitution into the preceding identity proves the claimed corrected error formula.
